name: Enzyme Inhibition
what: Enzyme inhibitors are molecules that reduce or block enzyme activity. Competitive inhibitors bind to the active site, while non-competitive inhibitors bind to the allosteric site and change the shape of the active site.
why: Inhibition is a key mechanism for regulating metabolism. It is also the basis for many drugs and pesticides — understanding inhibition types allows researchers to design molecules that target specific enzymes.

items.title: I can define competitive inhibition
items.what: Competitive inhibition occurs when a molecule with a similar shape to the substrate binds to the active site of the enzyme, blocking the substrate from binding. The inhibitor and substrate compete for the same site.
items.why: Competitive inhibition is a controllable and reversible form of enzyme regulation — its effect can be overcome by increasing substrate concentration, which has practical implications for drug design.
items.example: Ibuprofen acts as a competitive inhibitor of the enzyme COX (cyclooxygenase). It has a shape similar to the natural substrate arachidonic acid and blocks the active site, reducing the production of prostaglandins that cause inflammation.

items.title: I can define non-competitive inhibition
items.what: Non-competitive inhibition occurs when an inhibitor binds to the allosteric site (not the active site). This causes the active site to change shape so the substrate can no longer bind, reducing enzyme activity.
items.why: Non-competitive inhibition cannot be overcome by adding more substrate, making it a more absolute form of inhibition and a distinct mechanism from competitive inhibition.
items.example: Some nerve agents (such as organophosphates used as pesticides) bind to the allosteric site of acetylcholinesterase. The active site deforms and the enzyme can no longer break down the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, causing a dangerous build-up.

items.title: I can explain the effect of competitive inhibition on the rate of enzyme activity
items.what: A competitive inhibitor reduces enzyme activity by occupying active sites. However, increasing substrate concentration can outcompete the inhibitor and restore the rate of reaction toward its uninhibited maximum.
items.why: The reversibility of competitive inhibition has direct consequences for how drugs work in the body — dose and concentration of both drug and substrate matter.
items.example: If a competitive inhibitor is present and substrate concentration is doubled, the substrate molecules are more likely to reach and bind the active site before the inhibitor does. The rate of reaction increases compared to when substrate concentration was lower.

items.title: I can explain the effect of non-competitive inhibition on the rate of enzyme activity
items.what: A non-competitive inhibitor reduces enzyme activity by deforming the active site via the allosteric site. Increasing substrate concentration does not restore activity because the active site shape is altered regardless of how much substrate is present.
items.why: This makes non-competitive inhibitors particularly powerful as regulatory molecules or drugs — their effect is not diluted by increasing substrate levels.
items.example: In an experiment comparing competitive and non-competitive inhibitors, doubling the substrate concentration restores rate toward normal for the competitive inhibitor. For the non-competitive inhibitor, the rate remains depressed at approximately the same level regardless of substrate added.

items.title: I can compare competitive and non-competitive inhibition
items.what: Both types reduce enzyme activity by preventing the substrate from binding to the active site. Competitive inhibitors bind directly to the active site; non-competitive inhibitors bind to the allosteric site. Only competitive inhibition can be overcome by increasing substrate concentration.
items.why: Being able to compare both types is a common extended-response requirement and is necessary for interpreting graphs where substrate concentration is varied.
items.example: On a rate-versus-substrate-concentration graph, a competitive inhibitor shifts the curve right (higher substrate needed to reach the same rate) but the maximum rate is eventually reached. A non-competitive inhibitor lowers the maximum rate achievable, regardless of substrate concentration.

items.title: I can describe how competitive and non-competitive inhibition can be used in rational drug design
items.what: Rational drug design uses knowledge of an enzyme's active site or allosteric site to engineer molecules that selectively inhibit that enzyme. Competitive inhibitors mimic the substrate shape; non-competitive inhibitors are designed to bind the allosteric site.
items.why: Many modern medicines — including antibiotics, antivirals, and cancer treatments — work by inhibiting specific enzymes. Understanding the mechanism allows researchers to design more effective and selective drugs.
items.example: Researchers studying a bacterium that causes stomach disease could design a competitive inhibitor shaped like the substrate of the bacterium's critical enzyme, blocking its active site. Alternatively, they could design a non-competitive inhibitor targeting the allosteric site, permanently deforming the active site and stopping the enzyme regardless of substrate levels in the stomach environment.
